processing: Standard sheng: withered, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or sold loose.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as with other Yiwu village tea.
appearance_dry: Long, dark green large leaf with some buds, as usual for Yiwu.
taste_profile: No specific tasting record stands out for this village; typical of Yiwu, expect a soft, sweet broth with floral notes and little bitterness.

brewing.notes: Yiwu-style tea tolerates slightly longer steeps than strong Bulang teas.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as single-village sheng, usually spring. One published spring list gave 1,600 to 2,000 yuan/kg. As with other Yiwu villages, the name is easy to put on a label, so a seller's account of where the leaf came from matters.
description:
Luoshuidong is one of the villages of Yiwu, listed among the seven villages and eight hamlets people use to divide this famous mountain. It belongs to the Gumanche grouping alongside Mahei, Guafengzhai, Wangong and Yishangmo.

Nothing particular is documented about how the tea is made here. It should be read as ordinary sun-dried sheng, sold by village.

For taste, Yiwu's general description is the honest guide: soft water, sweetness, floral notes and low bitterness. A Luoshuidong character separate from that has not really been pinned down, so it is a good one to compare side by side with a Mahei.

Buy with a stated year and village. Yiwu names carry a premium, which makes small village labels easy to misuse.
history: Luoshuidong is recorded as one of the Yiwu villages with concentrated old tea gardens, and Yiwu itself was a main collecting point for the Qing-era tea trade. Little is documented about this village in particular, including when its tea first sold under its own name.
